card.title: DUG IN
card.text: Deal 1 damage to a unit. Shuffle SHIFTING DOCTRINE into your deck.
card.flavorText: As US forces advanced across the Pacific, Japanese defenders adapted with increasingly complex fortifications. Early in the war, Japanese doctrine stressed offensive action, but by 1943 the realities of Allied firepower and supply disruption forced a shift to static defense. On islands like Tarawa, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa, Japanese troops dug deep and built strong. Lacking concrete and steel, they turned to local materials. Coconut logs, coral blocks, oil barrels and sand-filled crates became bunkers, rifle pits and anti-tank obstacles. Positions were camouflaged with palm fronds or buried. On Iwo Jima, over 16 miles of tunnels connected hidden artillery and machine gun nests. Reverse slope defenses and dummy installations confused Allied spotters. The aim was not to stop landings at the beach but to kill the enemy after they landed. Each position was built to absorb artillery and protect crews from grenades, with overlapping fields of fire and concealed exits. These defenses stalled Allied attacks for weeks, inflicting high casualties. At Okinawa, over 60 miles of tunnels housed an entire army underground. Japan's dug-in strategy turned small islands into fortresses and made every yard of ground costly.
